blocks.text: She deals harshly with her young, as if they were not hers] The Chaldee renders it very differently: שיחנא על בניא דלא דילה, She broods over young that are not hers, that is, over the eggs of others, from which chicks may emerge. The Syriac has ܐܣܓܝܬ, she multiplies young not her own. The Arabic follows the same sense, and it describes the habits of the ostrich very well; of it Damir says: متي وجدت بيضة نعامة اخري تحضنها وتنسي بيضها [matā wajadat bayḍat naʿāma ukhrā taḥḍinuhā wa-tansā bayḍahā] If she comes upon the eggs of another ostrich, she broods them and forgets her own. Yet the Hebrew does not bear this rendering. Pagninus has: He makes her forget her young, in which they will not be. This I do not understand. Junius has: God, parching, hatches her young by another's work; that is, by the heat of the sun He warms the eggs which the ostrich had laid in the sand, until the chicks are hatched, as he also says in his Notes. For since he saw this asserted about the ostrich by learned men, he tried to bend the Hebrew text in that direction. But the simplest rendering is the one we have given, and it is therefore also the most ancient: She deals harshly with her young. In Hebrew, הקשיח בניה. The verb הקשיח occurs only here and in these words of Esa. LXIII, 17. Why hast thou let us stray from thy ways, O Lord, and תקשיח לבנו מיראתך, hardened our heart from thy fear? There the Septuagint has Ἐσκλήρυνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν [Esklērynas tas kardias hēmōn]; and Jerome, Thou hast hardened our heart? Nor do the Syriac and the Arabic differ. For קשח, with Cheth, is the same as הקשה, with He, except that in the former the stronger aspiration seems to intensify the meaning. So also in Arabic قسي [qasā] means to be hard, but قسح [qasaḥa] to be very hard and to be rigid. Hence قساح [qassāḥ] hyena, because it has a rigid neck, not flexible in any way. And رمح قاسح [rumḥ qāsiḥ] is a hard and rigid spear, like the spear of Lausus, of which the Poet speaks in book 10 of the Aeneid:
He comes up, and strikes Dryops from afar with his rigid spear.

Hence, then, applied to the mind, قسح [qasaḥa] or קשח means to be hard and unbending in mind; and הקשיח means either to be hardened or to deal harshly with someone ^{(3)}. Accordingly Jerome here has: She was hard toward her young. And Augustine: She hardened herself against her young. And the Greeks: Ἀπεσκλήρυνε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς [Apesklēryne ta tekna autēs], that is, τὴν περὶ τὰ τέκνα φυσικὴν στοργήν [tēn peri ta tekna physikēn storgēn]: She hardened her natural affection toward her young, as Olympiodorus rightly explains. To this belong these words of Jeremiah, Thren. IV, 3: The daughter of my people is cruel, [II, 860] like the ostriches in the desert. So too the fact that the ostrich is called תחמס in Hebrew and ظليم [ẓalīm] in Arabic, that is, impious, unjust, as we have already shown above ^{c)}. That the masculine verb הקשיח is used here for the feminine will surprise only someone who does not know how frequent this change of gender is in Hebrew idiom, especially with animals. Thus Esa. XIV, 11. תחתיך יצע רמה ומכסיך תולעה, Beneath thee the worm is spread, and the maggot covers thee. There the nouns are feminine, but the verbs masculine. Conversely, in Exod. VIII, 2. [var. 6.] ותעל הצפרדע, And the frog came up; and in verse 14 [var. 16], ותהי הכנים, And there was the louse: feminine verbs are joined to masculine nouns. Kimchi, on Isaiah, says this is the custom of Scripture [col. 255] when it speaks not of this or that animal, but על דרך כלל, universally, of the whole species, as here of the ostrich. Her young, in Hebrew בניה, her sons, that is, the eggs from which chicks would have emerged had she brooded them. They are therefore called sons δυνωτικῶς [dynōtikōs]. Compare that line of Martial, book 9, Epigram 42:
What you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.

As if they were not hers] In Hebrew, ללא לה. In full it would be כאשר לא יהיו לה, as in Iob. X, 19. כאשר לא הייתי, As if I had not been ^{(4)}. But in this book the style is sometimes very concise, because it is not prose but verse. And this antithesis has its own charm: her young, as though not hers. Compare that of Paul, 1 Cor. VII, 30: Οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες [Hoi klaiontes hōs mē klaiontes, kai hoi chairontes hōs mē chairontes], etc. Those who weep as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, etc. And Hebr. XI, 27. Τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν [Ton gar aoraton hōs horōn]: As seeing him who is invisible.
